result: A systematic review identified 4,274 records, of which 64 studies met inclusion criteria, contributing 9,631 specimens from adult and pediatric cases across 15 countries, including asymptomatic, presymptomatic, and symptomatic infections. Most contributing studies had low risk of bias according to a hybrid Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist.
evaluation: Claims C17-C22 describe the systematic review methodology and dataset characteristics. The numbers are clearly reported, the inclusion criteria are documented, and risk of bias assessment was performed. The systematic approach and transparent reporting support these descriptive claims.

result: Meta-regression analysis demonstrated a negative association between the dispersion parameter k and heterogeneity in respiratory viral load (rVL). Using low risk of bias studies, a strong negative association was found (p<0.001, r=-0.73), with each unit increase in standard deviation of rVL decreasing log(k) by -1.41 (95% CI: -1.78 to -1.03), suggesting broader heterogeneity in rVL facilitates greater overdispersion in SARS-CoV-2 transmissibility compared to A(H1N1)pdm09.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 present the core meta-regression findings with appropriate statistical tests, effect sizes, and confidence intervals. The analysis is shown in Figure 2 with clear methodology. The inference about overdispersion (C26) follows logically from the quantitative association, though causality cannot be definitively established from correlation alone.

result: Meta-analysis comparing expected respiratory viral loads showed that SARS-CoV-2 rVL was comparable to SARS-CoV-1 (p=0.111) but lower than A(H1N1)pdm09 (p=0.040).
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 report statistical comparisons from random-effects meta-analysis with appropriate p-values. The analysis is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. The statistical tests are appropriate for comparing mean estimates across viruses, though significant between-study heterogeneity was noted.

result: Subgroup analyses of COVID-19 cases showed that expected SARS-CoV-2 rVLs were similar between pediatric and adult cases (p=0.476) and between symptomatic/presymptomatic and asymptomatic infections (p=0.090). The rVL distributions had similar standard deviations (2.00-2.06 log10 copies/ml) across subgroups, indicating that age and symptomatology minimally influenced case variation in SARS-CoV-2 rVL.
evaluation: Claims C29-C30, C37-C38 present subgroup meta-analyses with appropriate statistical tests and distribution fitting shown in Figures 3 and 4B-C. The similar standard deviations across subgroups support the inference that age and symptomatology have minimal influence on heterogeneity. However, significant between-study heterogeneity was present, which may affect interpretation.

result: Respiratory viral loads for all three viruses best conformed to Weibull distributions. At the 90th case percentile, estimated rVL was 8.91 (95% CI: 8.83-9.00) log10 copies/ml for SARS-CoV-2 and 8.62 (8.47-8.76) log10 copies/ml for A(H1N1)pdm09. The standard deviation of the overall rVL distribution was 2.04 log10 copies/ml for SARS-CoV-2 and 1.45 log10 copies/ml for A(H1N1)pdm09, confirming broader heterogeneity for SARS-CoV-2.
evaluation: Claims C31-C36 describe distribution fitting results with appropriate goodness-of-fit tests (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and parameter estimates. The Weibull distribution was selected based on statistical testing, and the quantile estimates and standard deviations are clearly reported with confidence intervals. The comparison of heterogeneity follows directly from the standard deviation estimates.

result: A mechanistic model of SARS-CoV-2 kinetics estimated that each productively infected cell shed virus at 1.33 (95% CI: 0.74-1.93) copies/ml day⁻¹ and infected up to 9.25 susceptible cells. The turnover rate for infected cells was 0.71 (0.26-1.15) days⁻¹, and viral RNA half-life was 0.21 (0.11-2.75) days. The estimated incubation period was 5.38 days, and expected shedding duration was 25.1 DFSO. SARS-CoV-2 rVL increased exponentially after infection, peaked around 1 DFSO, then diminished exponentially.
evaluation: Claims C39-C45 present mechanistic modeling results with parameter estimates and confidence intervals shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4-5. The model achieved good fit (r²=0.84) and the estimated incubation period agrees with epidemiological findings (C43). However, the wide confidence interval for viral RNA half-life (C42) indicates substantial uncertainty in this parameter.

result: High SARS-CoV-2 rVLs increased from the presymptomatic period, peaked at 1 DFSO, then decreased towards the end of the first week of illness. At 1 DFSO, the 90th case percentile rVL was 9.84 (95% CI: 9.17-10.56) log10 copies/ml, an order of magnitude greater than the overall 90th percentile estimate. High rVLs between 1 and 5 DFSO were elevated above expected values from the overall distribution. Heterogeneity remained broad across the infectious period with standard deviations of 1.83-2.44 log10 copies/ml between -1 to 10 DFSO.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 describe temporal dynamics of rVL distributions across DFSO, supported by Weibull distribution fitting for each time point (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2H-S). The quantile estimates are provided with confidence intervals, and the temporal patterns are clearly visualized. The finding of persistent heterogeneity across the infectious period is well-supported by the standard deviation estimates.

result: Poisson modeling of virion partitioning into respiratory particles showed that when expelled by the mean COVID-19 case, aerosols (≤100 μm) were ≤3.16% (95% CI: 2.61-3.71%) likely to contain a virion, while droplets at 200 μm were 22.3% (21.4-23.2%) likely to contain one virion. For high case percentiles, likelihoods increased substantially: at the 80th percentile, aerosols were ≤87.9% (87.2-88.5%) likely to carry at least one virion, and at 1 DFSO for the 98th percentile, ≤98.8% (98.1-99.4%) of buoyant aerosols contained at least one viable SARS-CoV-2 copy. High percentile cases expelled droplets containing tens to thousands of virions.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 present Poisson modeling results for virion partitioning. While the mathematical framework is appropriate and results are shown in Figure 5A-B and supplements, the model assumes a viability proportion of 0.1% based on influenza data and limited SARS-CoV-2 culture studies. This critical assumption introduces substantial uncertainty, as the authors acknowledge that viability proportion remains under investigation (C124). The model also assumes Poisson partitioning based on volume, which may not capture surface-area dependent mechanisms.

result: Modeling of respiratory activities showed that singing shed virions more rapidly than talking based on increased aerosol emission, though talking loudly emitted aerosols at similar rates to singing. Talking and singing shed virions significantly more rapidly than breathing, and each cough shed similar quantities as a minute of talking. Talking, singing, and coughing expelled virions at comparable proportions via droplets (55.6-59.4%) and aerosols (40.6-44.4%), while breathing did so predominantly via aerosols. Short-range aerosols mediated most virions (79.2-81.9%) shed via aerosols while talking normally and coughing, whereas singing or talking loudly increased the proportion carried by buoyant (14.5%) and long-range (17.5%) aerosols.
evaluation: Claims C57-C64 combine rVL distributions with published respiratory particle emission profiles (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). While the integration is mathematically sound and results are shown in Figure 5C-G, the model relies on particle emission data from limited studies (Johnson et al. 2011, Morawska et al. 2009) that may not represent population variability. The authors acknowledge that emission rates and size distributions differ across studies and individuals, and that individual variation in respiratory capacity is not captured.

result: Total SARS-CoV-2 shedding rates across respiratory activities spanned ≥8.48 orders of magnitude on each DFSO and 11.0 orders of magnitude cumulatively from -1 to 10 DFSO, indicating that many COVID-19 cases inherently presented minimal transmission risk while highly infectious individuals shed considerable quantities. For the 98th case percentile at 1 DFSO, singing expelled 313 (95% CI: 37.5-3158) virions/min, talking emitted 293 (35.1-2664) virions/min, breathing exhaled 1.54 (0.18-15.5) virions/min, and coughing discharged 249 (29.8-25111) virions/cough. Adult, pediatric, symptomatic/presymptomatic, and asymptomatic COVID-19 subgroups presented similar distributions for shedding virions.
evaluation: Claims C65-C74 present integrated modeling results combining rVL heterogeneity with respiratory particle emission (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The extreme heterogeneity (11 orders of magnitude) is mathematically derived from the model, but the very wide confidence intervals (e.g., C69: 37.5-3158 virions/min) indicate substantial uncertainty. The model compounds uncertainties from viability proportion, particle emission profiles, and rVL distributions. While the qualitative conclusion about heterogeneity is supported, the quantitative estimates should be interpreted cautiously.

result: Comparative modeling showed that 62.9% of A(H1N1)pdm09 cases were infectious via aerosols within 24 hr of talking loudly or singing, compared to 48.0% of COVID-19 cases. Only 61.4% of COVID-19 cases shed ≥1 virion via either droplets or aerosols in 24 hr of talking loudly or singing, suggesting at least 38.6% presented negligible transmission risk. The proportion decreased with higher thresholds: 55.8%, 42.5%, and 25.0% of COVID-19 cases shed ≥2, ≥10, and ≥100 virions, respectively. While a greater proportion of A(H1N1)pdm09 cases were inherently infectious, 18.8% of COVID-19 cases shed virions more rapidly than A(H1N1)pdm09 cases, with highly infectious COVID-19 cases expelling virions at rates up to 1-2 orders of magnitude greater than their A(H1N1)pdm09 counterparts.
evaluation: Claims C77-C90 compare infectiousness between COVID-19 and A(H1N1)pdm09 using the shedding model (Figure 5—figure supplement 4-5). The comparison assumes the same viability proportion (0.1%) for both viruses and uses the HID50 of 1-3 virions for influenza as a threshold. However, the human infectious dose for SARS-CoV-2 is unknown (acknowledged by authors), making the threshold-based comparisons (C80-C85) speculative. The qualitative patterns are supported by the data, but quantitative conclusions about proportions of infectious cases depend on unvalidated assumptions.

result: The authors conclude that broader heterogeneity in rVL facilitates greater overdispersion for SARS-CoV-2 than A(H1N1)pdm09, explaining why many COVID-19 cases infect no one while highly infectious cases can shed tens to thousands of virions/min (especially between 1-5 DFSO), potentiating superspreading events. In comparison, a greater proportion of A(H1N1)pdm09 cases are infectious but shed at low rates, consistent with more uniform transmission during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. The authors suggest heterogeneity in rVL may be generally associated with overdispersion for viral respiratory infections, and that rVL distribution can serve as an early correlate for transmission patterns during novel virus outbreaks.
evaluation: Claims C91-C99 synthesize the main findings and interpretations. The association between rVL heterogeneity and overdispersion is supported by the meta-regression (C23-C26). The mechanistic explanation linking heterogeneity to differential infectiousness is supported by the modeling results, though with the uncertainties noted above. The comparison with A(H1N1)pdm09 transmission patterns (C95-C96) is supported by cited literature. The broader generalization (C97-C98) is appropriately framed as a suggestion based on three viruses. The model estimates align with clinical findings (C94).

result: Viral load kinetics showed that rVL tends to peak at 1 DFSO and be elevated for 1-5 DFSO, coinciding with the period of highest attack rates among close contacts. This indicates transmission risk is greatest near and soon after illness rather than in the presymptomatic period, consistent with large tracing studies (6.4-12.6% of secondary infections from presymptomatic transmission) rather than early temporal models (~44%). On average, SARS-CoV-2 reaches diagnostic concentrations 1.54-3.17 days after respiratory infection (-3.84 to -2.21 DFSO), assuming assay detection limits of 1-3 log10 copies/ml.
evaluation: Claims C102-C107 interpret the kinetic modeling results in epidemiological context. The temporal pattern of rVL (C102) is supported by the mechanistic model (Figure 4D). The concordance with contact tracing attack rates (C103) is supported by citation. The inference about transmission risk timing (C104) follows logically from the kinetic data, and the comparison with tracing studies (C105-C106) appropriately contextualizes the findings. The diagnostic threshold calculation (C107) is a straightforward extrapolation from the model, though it should be validated prospectively.

result: Coughing, a common symptom of COVID-19, sheds considerable numbers of virions via droplets and short-range aerosols, making symptomatic infections more contagious than asymptomatic ones. This provides one reason why asymptomatic cases transmit SARS-CoV-2 at lower relative rates, especially in close contact, despite similar rVLs. Children (48-54% with cough) may be less contagious than adults (68-80% with cough) based on symptomatology rather than rVL.
evaluation: Claims C108-C114 integrate modeling results with clinical symptom data. The modeling shows coughing increases shedding (Figure 5F), and symptom prevalence data are cited (C108, C112-C113). The inference that symptomatic cases are more contagious (C110) follows logically, and the explanation for lower asymptomatic transmission (C111) is supported by cited studies. The comparison between children and adults (C114) appropriately attributes differences to symptomatology given similar rVLs (C29). However, the model does not account for other behavioral differences between symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals.

result: Conversely, coughing sheds few virions via smaller aerosols, while singing and talking loudly allow highly infectious cases to shed tens to hundreds of SARS-CoV-2 virions/min via long-range and buoyant aerosols.
evaluation: Claims C115-C116 describe differential shedding patterns across particle sizes and activities, supported by the modeling results in Figure 5C-G. The particle size distribution profiles for different activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) show that coughing generates fewer small aerosols relative to larger particles, while singing/loud talking generate more small aerosols. Combined with rVL distributions, this supports the stated patterns.

result: The systematic search found limited studies reporting quantitative specimen measurements from the presymptomatic period, potentially introducing sampling bias. Semiquantitative metrics (cycle thresholds) were excluded because they cannot be compared on an absolute scale due to batch effects.
evaluation: Claims C117-C118 acknowledge study limitations. The limited presymptomatic data is evident in the dataset (C21: only 28 presymptomatic specimens). The exclusion of Ct values is justified by citation (Han et al., 2021) and is a methodologically sound decision given known batch effects in qRT-PCR. These are appropriate limitations to acknowledge.

result: Severe COVID-19 is associated with high, persistent SARS-CoV-2 shedding in the lower respiratory tract, and since small particles are typically generated there, severe cases may expel higher quantities of virions via smaller aerosols.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120 cite literature on severe disease and particle generation sites. However, C121 is speculative, as acknowledged by the authors' use of "may." The model does not include data from severe cases or differentiate by disease severity, and the mechanism linking lower respiratory tract shedding to aerosol generation is not directly tested. This is appropriately framed as speculation.

result: Individual variation in viral viability exists, with some patients shedding SARS-CoV-2 with diminishing viability soon after symptom onset while others produce replication-competent virus for weeks. The proportion of viable SARS-CoV-2 in respiratory particles and how case characteristics or environmental factors influence it remains under investigation.
evaluation: Claims C122-C124 acknowledge uncertainty in viral viability, supported by citations to relevant studies. This is an important limitation affecting the modeling results (C52-C90), as the assumed 0.1% viability proportion is a population-level estimate that may not capture individual variation. The authors appropriately acknowledge this uncertainty.

result: While talking, singing, and coughing, SARS-CoV-2 is shed via droplets (55.6-59.4%), short-range aerosols (30.1-34.9%), long-range aerosols (7.7-8.3%), and buoyant aerosols (0.01-6.5%). With short durations of stay in well-ventilated areas, exposure risk for both droplets and aerosols remains correlated with proximity. The authors recommend strategies to limit crowd numbers and duration of stay while reinforcing distancing, low-voice amplitudes, and mask usage, recognizing well-ventilated settings as lower-risk venues. Immediate, sustained self-isolation upon illness is crucial to curb transmission from symptomatic cases.
evaluation: Claims C125-C129 synthesize modeling results into public health recommendations. The particle size distribution (C125) is from modeling (C61-C64). The statement about proximity and ventilation (C126) is supported by citations. The recommendations (C127-C129) follow logically from the findings about temporal dynamics (peak at 1 DFSO), activity-based shedding, and the role of aerosols. These are reasonable evidence-based recommendations, though they extend beyond what the data directly demonstrate.

result: For nasopharyngeal swabs in 1 ml transport media, ≥7.14 (95% CI: 7.07-7.22) log10 copies/ml corresponds to the top 20% of COVID-19 cases for variants before August 2020. The authors propose that qRT-PCR can triage contact tracing by prioritizing high viral load patients, which may identify asymptomatic and presymptomatic infections more efficiently.
evaluation: Claim C130 provides a quantitative threshold from the rVL distribution (80th percentile). However, claims C131-C132 propose a novel contact tracing strategy that has not been tested or validated. While the logic is sound (high rVL cases are more infectious based on the model), the practical effectiveness, feasibility, and potential unintended consequences of this approach are unknown. This is appropriately framed as a proposal but requires prospective validation.
